summary: An author's study of how long it takes to publish an idea as an RFC, from the first individual draft to publication. It examines a random sample of RFCs approved in 2018, with random samples from 2008 and 1998 for comparison, looking at their histories and delays.

plainLanguage.summary: Someone checked how long it takes for an idea to become an official Internet document, by looking at a bunch of examples, and wrote down what slowed things.

questions: how long does it take to publish an rfc
why are rfc publication delays long
what is the auth48 phase in rfc publication
how are rfc publication delays measured
subtitle: A study of how long Internet standards take to publish.

tldr.problem: The IETF RFC publication process is long and complex; people wonder what causes delays and whether the process is getting faster or slower.
tldr.mechanism: An author examined 20 random RFCs published in 2018 in detail, tracking dates from the first draft to publication and breaking delays into working group, IETF review, and RFC production phases. They compared to random samples from 2008 and 1998.
tldr.outcome: Average 2018 RFC took 3 years 4 months: 2 years 9 months in working group, 3-4 months for IETF review and RFC production. AUTH48 editing is the main source of variability. RFCs take about 3 times longer in 2018 than 1998, but about the same as 2008.

today: RFC 8963 is an Informational document published in January 2021 reporting on a study performed in 2019-2020. It presents a snapshot of RFC publication delays as they stood in 2018. The study has become a reference point for discussions about IETF process efficiency and the factors that contribute to the length of the standardization process.

sections.title: The Study and Its Method
sections.content:
This RFC reports on a study of RFC publication delays. The author randomly selected 20 RFCs that were approved for publication in 2018, examined their history in detail, and compared them to random samples of 20 RFCs each from 2008 and 1998. The study used the IETF Datatracker (the database that records all RFC history) to measure key dates and break down the total time into phases: working group processing, IETF consensus and review, and RFC production and publication (including the AUTH48 author review phase).

The sample is small (20 out of 209 RFCs published in 2018), so the results show trends rather than definitive statistics. The author also examined citation counts from Semantic Scholar to see if the number of times an RFC is cited in academic papers correlates with how widely the protocol is actually deployed.
sections.plainLanguage: An author picked 20 RFCs at random, looked at when each step happened (draft submission, working group approval, IESG approval, publishing), and compared the times to RFCs from 10 and 20 years ago.

sections.title: Overall Publication Time
sections.content:
The average RFC in the 2018 sample took 3 years and 4 months from the first draft to publication. This time breaks down as follows: 2 years and 9 months in the working group, 3 to 4 months for IETF consensus review and IESG assessment, and 3 to 4 months for RFC production including the AUTH48 phase.

The variation is large. The shortest RFC took only 9 months (an opinion piece on DNS submitted to the Independent Stream), while the longest took 6.5 years (a TLS-related draft that failed to achieve consensus in its working group, was abandoned, then years later resubmitted through the Independent Submission stream). Excluding Independent Stream RFCs (which are typically faster), the average is 3 years 4 months.

Comparing across decades reveals that RFC publication has slowed over time. In 1998, RFCs were published 3 to 4 times faster than in 2018. However, delays in 2018 are similar to those in 2008, suggesting the slowdown happened between 1998 and 2008, with little further change since.
sections.plainLanguage: Most RFCs take about 3 years and 4 months to publish. In 1998, they were published much faster. The time hasn't changed much between 2008 and 2018, so the slowdown happened a while ago.

sections.title: Where the Delays Happen
sections.content:
The biggest source of delay is the working group phase: about 80% of the total time. The working group must reach consensus on the details of the protocol or specification. This includes a period before the draft is formally adopted (averaging about 9 months) and a longer period after adoption (averaging about 22 months).

The IETF consensus and review phase accounts for about 10% of delays: roughly 3-4 months. This includes the IETF Last Call (where all IETF participants review the draft), IESG (Internet Engineering Steering Group) review, and directorate reviews for technical quality.

The RFC production phase accounts for the remaining 10%: roughly 3-4 months. This includes the RFC Editor's initial editing, the AUTH48 phase (where authors review and approve the RFC Production Center's final edits), and final publication. The AUTH48 phase is especially variable: it nominally should take 2 days but averages over a month. The main reasons are time zone differences across multiple authors, authors rejecting proposed edits and requesting changes, and authors not giving the task high priority.

Document length and copy editing requirements correlate with production delays. Longer documents and those requiring more editing take longer. The number of authors also tends to increase delays, possibly due to coordination overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Most time (80%) is spent in the working group debating the details. Next (10%) is the IETF reviewing it. Last (10%) is the RFC Production Center fixing up the document. The longest delays come from authors and editors going back and forth on final changes.

sections.title: Citation Counts and Deployment
sections.content:
The author measured how many times each RFC was cited in academic papers using Semantic Scholar. The results show TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) was by far the most cited (418 citations as of October 2019), followed by the CUBIC congestion control algorithm (RFC 8312, with 25 citations). Most other RFCs in the sample had fewer than 5 citations.

Citation counts indicate academic interest but correlate only loosely with actual deployment. RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3) is heavily cited and widely deployed. RFC 8312 (CUBIC) is widely implemented in operating systems. But several other RFCs with zero citations in academic papers are also widely deployed (like RFC 8362 on OSPF extensions, which router vendors implement). Conversely, some RFCs with modest citations may have limited real-world use.

Comparing 1998 and 2008 RFCs shows older, more established protocols accumulate more citations over time. However, recent deployment data (not academic citation counts) is a better indicator of actual usage. The author suggests counting web references (how many times an RFC is linked on websites) might complement citation counts as a measure of impact.
sections.plainLanguage: Popular protocols like TLS get cited a lot in academic papers. But citation counts don't always match real-world use: some widely-deployed protocols are barely mentioned in papers. Web references might be a better measure than academic citations.

sections.title: Key Observations and Future Work
sections.content:
The study reveals several insights. First, working group delays dominate: they account for 80% of total publication time, so any effort to speed up RFC publication should focus on working group processes.

Second, AUTH48 is unpredictable: while the RFC Editor's initial editing averages 2 months, AUTH48 (author review) varies wildly, with some RFCs taking 3+ months. This suggests the process is not just about document quality but also depends on author availability and responsiveness.

Third, the Independent Submission stream is faster than the IETF stream (except for anomalies like RFC 8492, which spent years in working group before being submitted independently). Independent documents average 1-2 years from submission to publication.

Fourth, process metrics might not directly measure value. Long delays might indicate high-quality consensus-building rather than inefficiency. Fast publication might mean insufficient review.

The author identifies potential next steps: automating delay measurements using Datatracker data, studying abandoned drafts (which would reveal the IETF's ability to triage failed efforts), and adding detailed instrumentation to track what causes long working group delays.
sections.plainLanguage: The main takeaway: if you want RFCs published faster, focus on speeding up working group discussions, not RFC editing. But it's unclear if faster is better—longer delays might just mean more careful review.
